When the stressor truly can't be changed, it's often the most helpful choice.

questions.q: Self-determination theory identifies three basic psychological needs:
o: safety, love, esteem
Safety, love and esteem are levels of Maslow's hierarchy.
drive, incentive, arousal
Drive, incentive and arousal are names of separate motivation theories.
autonomy, competence, and relatedness
Correct: autonomy, competence and relatedness are the needs that build intrinsic motivation.
extrinsic, intrinsic, amotivation
Those are types of motivation, not needs.
questions.x: Self-determination theory says people feel most motivated from the inside, called intrinsic motivation, when three basic needs are met. Autonomy is feeling that your choices are your own. Competence is feeling skilled and effective. Relatedness is feeling connected to other people. The easy mistake is to grab Maslow's hierarchy, since it's also about needs. But safety, love and esteem are Maslow's levels, not the three needs of self-determination theory. Intrinsic, extrinsic and amotivation are types of motivation, not needs.

questions.q: Bilateral removal of the temporal lobes including the amygdala in monkeys produced:
o: heightened aggression and fear
Fear and aggression go down, not up.
loss of vision
The monkeys can still see; they just don't recognize what objects are.
inability to form new declarative memories only
The defining signs are emotional and behavioral, not just a memory problem.
tameness, loss of fear, and hyperorality
Correct: this is Klüver-Bucy syndrome.
questions.x: Removing both temporal lobes, including the amygdala, causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome. The amygdala is a small almond-shaped structure that handles fear and aggression. Without it, monkeys become tame and lose their fear, even of things they should avoid. They also explore objects by putting them in their mouths (hyperorality) and show increased sexual behavior (hypersexuality). They can still see, but they have trouble recognizing what objects are. The easy mistake is assuming amygdala damage would make an animal more fearful or aggressive. It does the opposite.

questions.q: Researchers compare a trait's concordance in monozygotic twins reared apart with that in dizygotic twins reared together. Higher concordance in the monozygotic pairs would most directly suggest that:
o: genetic factors contribute to variation in the trait
Correct: identical twins raised apart still match more, so shared genes must be contributing.
shared family environment is the sole determinant of the trait
The MZ twins grew up in different homes, so family environment can't explain their similarity.
the trait is fully determined by genes with no environmental input
Showing genes contribute isn't the same as genes deciding everything.
the trait arises from random developmental error
Random developmental errors wouldn't make identical twins match more often in a consistent way.
questions.x: Concordance is how often both twins have a trait when one does. Monozygotic (MZ, identical) twins share nearly all their genes; dizygotic (DZ, fraternal) twins share about half. This setup is clever: the MZ twins were raised apart, so they didn't share a home, while the DZ twins did. If the MZ twins still match more often, a shared home can't explain it. Their shared genes can. So the trait has a genetic influence. Careful, though: that doesn't mean genes decide everything. Unless MZ twins match 100% of the time, environment still plays a part.

questions.q: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia proposes that positive symptoms such as hallucinations result from:
o: deficient acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions
Low acetylcholine at the nerve-muscle junction causes muscle weakness, not hallucinations.
loss of GABA-mediated inhibition in the spinal cord
Losing GABA's calming effect in the spinal cord causes muscle spasms, not psychosis.
excess dopamine activity in mesolimbic pathways
Correct: too much dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway drives hallucinations, and antipsychotics block D₂ receptors.
depleted serotonin in the raphe nuclei only
Low serotonin is linked to depression, and it isn't the dopamine hypothesis.
questions.x: Schizophrenia has positive symptoms, things added to normal experience, like hallucinations (sensing things that aren't there) and delusions (strongly held false beliefs). The dopamine hypothesis says these come from too much dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway, a dopamine circuit deep in the brain. Two clues support it. Antipsychotic drugs work by blocking D₂ dopamine receptors. And drugs that boost dopamine, like amphetamines, can cause psychosis. Don't mix this up with Parkinson disease, which is caused by too little dopamine in a different pathway.

questions.q: Participants injected with epinephrine reported anger or euphoria depending on a confederate's behavior. This supports which theory?
o: James-Lange theory, in which arousal alone defines the emotion
James-Lange has no labeling step. The same shot should have produced the same emotion.
Two-factor theory, in which arousal is cognitively labeled
Correct: emotion is arousal plus a label taken from the situation, here the confederate's behavior.
Cannon-Bard theory, in which emotion precedes arousal
Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion happen at the same time, with no labeling from context.
the facial feedback hypothesis only
Facial feedback is about facial expressions shaping emotion, not injections and social cues.
questions.x: This is the famous Schachter-Singer study, and it supports their two-factor theory of emotion. The theory says an emotion needs two things: body arousal (racing heart, shaky hands) and a mental label for that arousal, which you pick up from the situation. Everyone got the same epinephrine (adrenaline) shot, so they all had the same arousal. What changed was a confederate, someone secretly working with the researchers, who acted either angry or giddy. People labeled their arousal to match, feeling angry or euphoric. James-Lange can't explain this, because it says arousal alone sets the emotion, so the same shot should feel the same.

questions.q: A person who has two or more distinct personality states and gaps in memory for everyday events is most likely diagnosed with:
o: dissociative identity disorder
Correct: two or more distinct identities plus memory gaps beyond normal forgetting.
borderline personality disorder
Borderline means unstable mood, relationships and self-image, not separate identities.
schizophrenia
Schizophrenia involves hallucinations and delusions, not split identities.
schizoid personality disorder
Schizoid means being detached from people with little emotion, not separate identities.
questions.x: This is dissociative identity disorder (DID). Dissociative disorders involve a break in the normal links between memory, awareness and identity. In DID, a person has two or more distinct identities or personality states, and memory gaps that go well beyond ordinary forgetting, including gaps for everyday events. The classic trap is schizophrenia. The name sounds like 'split mind,' so people think it means split personality. It doesn't. Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder, with hallucinations and delusions, and the person has one identity.

questions.q: A person who repeatedly lies, violates others' rights, and shows no remorse most likely has:
o: antisocial personality disorder
Correct: a lasting pattern of lying, violating others' rights and feeling no remorse.
avoidant personality disorder
Avoidant means shyness and fear of rejection, not harming others.
dependent personality disorder
Dependent means an excessive need to be cared for and going along with others.
obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
OCPD means perfectionism and rigid control, not violating others' rights.
questions.x: This is antisocial personality disorder. It's a long-lasting pattern of ignoring and violating other people's rights: lying, conning, breaking rules and laws, and feeling no remorse or guilt about it. It's in Cluster B, the dramatic, emotional and impulsive group of personality disorders. In everyday speech 'antisocial' can mean shy or unsociable, but in psychology it means acting against society. The tempting wrong answers are other personality disorders like avoidant and dependent, but those are about fear and needing others, not harming them.

questions.q: A group of moderately cautious investors becomes much more cautious after discussion. This is:
o: groupthink
Groupthink is hiding doubts to keep group harmony, not a stronger version of the starting lean.
group polarization
Correct: discussion pushed the group further in the direction it already leaned.
conformity to an external norm
Conformity to an outside standard isn't the same as the group strengthening its own lean.
social loafing
Social loafing is putting in less effort in a group. It doesn't shift opinions.
questions.x: This is group polarization. When a group discusses something, its average opinion tends to get more extreme in the direction it already leaned. These investors started out moderately cautious. After talking it over, they became much more cautious. If they had started out leaning risky, discussion would have made them riskier. A common trap is assuming groups always settle on a middle-of-the-road view. They often don't. Groupthink is another tempting pick, but groupthink is about members hiding their doubts to keep the peace, which isn't described here.

questions.q: Individuals boost self-esteem by viewing their own group more favorably than other groups. This reflects:
o: the contact hypothesis
The contact hypothesis is about when contact between groups reduces prejudice.
social identity theory with ingroup bias
Correct: groups are part of your sense of self, so favoring your own group raises self-esteem.
the Barnum effect
The Barnum effect is believing vague descriptions, like horoscopes, apply to you personally.
self-perception theory
Self-perception theory says we figure out our attitudes by watching our own behavior.
questions.x: Social identity theory, from Henri Tajfel and John Turner, says part of who you are comes from the groups you belong to. Your ingroup is your own group, like your team, school or country. An outgroup is any other group. Because your group is part of your sense of self, seeing your group as better makes you feel better about yourself. Favoring your own group like this is called ingroup bias. That's exactly what the question describes: boosting self-esteem by rating your own group above others.

questions.q: According to Cooley, a person develops a self-concept by:
o: internalizing instinctual drives
Instinctual drives belong to Freud's theory, not Cooley's social idea.
comparing to an ideal self only
Comparing yourself to an ideal self is Rogers's idea, not Cooley's mirror of others.
imagining how others perceive and judge them
Correct: Cooley's looking-glass self builds your self-concept from imagining others' views and judgments.
observing physiological arousal
Reading your own body arousal belongs to emotion theories, not Cooley.
questions.x: Charles Cooley called his idea the looking-glass self ('looking glass' is an old word for mirror). He said other people act like a mirror for us. You build your self-concept, your picture of who you are, in three steps. First, you imagine how you look to others. Second, you imagine how they judge what they see. Third, you feel something about yourself because of that, like pride or embarrassment. So the answer is imagining how others perceive and judge you. Don't confuse Cooley with George Herbert Mead, who described stages of learning to take other people's roles.

questions.q: A job candidate dresses carefully and emphasizes strengths to create a favorable image. This is:
o: fundamental attribution error
The fundamental attribution error is about how we judge others' behavior, not shaping your own image.
impression management
Correct: deliberately shaping how others see you, like dressing well and stressing strengths.
stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is doing worse from fear of confirming a stereotype, not shaping an image on purpose.
deindividuation
Deindividuation is losing self-awareness. This candidate is highly self-aware.
questions.x: This is impression management, also called self-presentation. It means deliberately shaping how other people see you. Dressing carefully for an interview and talking up your strengths are classic examples. Sociologist Erving Goffman compared it to acting on a stage: we choose what to show 'front stage' to an audience. Impression management doesn't have to mean lying. You can be completely honest and still choose what to highlight. Deindividuation is the opposite: it's losing self-awareness in an anonymous crowd, while this candidate is very aware of how she comes across.

questions.q: A manager assumes a very attractive employee is also competent and honest. This is the:
o: fundamental attribution error
The fundamental attribution error is about explaining behavior by personality instead of the situation.
just-world hypothesis
The just-world hypothesis is believing people get what they deserve.
halo effect
Correct: one good trait, attractiveness, leads to assuming other good traits like competence and honesty.
self-serving bias
Self-serving bias is crediting yourself for successes and blaming outside causes for failures.
questions.x: This is the halo effect. It's a thinking shortcut where one positive trait, like good looks, makes us assume a person has other good traits too, like competence and honesty. The good trait casts a 'halo' over everything else about them. The manager has no evidence the employee is skilled or honest, only that they're attractive. The halo effect is about judging one individual, which sets it apart from stereotyping, which is about a whole group. The reverse, where one bad trait colors everything, is sometimes called the horn effect.

questions.q: Parents praising boys for assertiveness and girls for helpfulness illustrates:
o: gender role socialization via reinforcement
Correct: different praise for boys and girls teaches them different gender roles.
genetic essentialism
Genetic essentialism says differences are inborn. Here they come from parents' praise.
classical conditioning of gender
Praise after a behavior is operant reinforcement, not classical conditioning's pairing of stimuli.
stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is doing worse when a negative stereotype is on your mind.
questions.x: This is gender role socialization through reinforcement. Socialization is how we learn our culture's roles and rules. Gender roles are the behaviors a society expects from boys and girls. Here, parents praise boys for being assertive and girls for being helpful. Praise is reinforcement: a reward after a behavior that makes it more likely to happen again. This is operant conditioning, learning from consequences. Giving different praise to boys and girls shapes them into different learned roles. The trap is treating these differences as inborn when the question shows them being taught.

questions.q: Slot machines pay out after unpredictable numbers of pulls, producing persistent responding. This is:
o: fixed-ratio schedule
Fixed ratio pays after a set number of pulls, giving bursts with pauses after each reward.
fixed-interval schedule
Fixed interval pays after a set time, so responding speeds up as that time nears.
variable-interval schedule
Variable interval depends on unpredictable time, not number of pulls, and gives slower steady rates.
variable-ratio schedule
Correct: unpredictable numbers of responses give fast, steady, persistent responding, like slot machines.
questions.x: This is a variable-ratio schedule. 'Ratio' means rewards depend on the number of responses (here, pulls). 'Variable' means that number changes unpredictably each time. Since any pull might be the winner, people pull fast and steadily, and they keep going long after losing streaks, which makes this schedule very hard to extinguish. The common trap is mixing up ratio schedules, which count responses, with interval schedules, which count time.

questions.q: A teenager begins to see herself as artistic because teachers and classmates consistently describe her that way and praise her drawings. Which concept best explains how her self-view developed?
o: Cooley's looking-glass self
Correct: her self-view grew from how others saw and judged her.
Freud's reaction formation
Reaction formation is a defense that shows the opposite of an unacceptable impulse.
Bandura's self-efficacy
Self-efficacy is belief in your ability at a task, not taking on others' views.
Erikson's moratorium
Moratorium is exploring without committing, not absorbing others' judgments.
questions.x: Charles Cooley's looking-glass self says we form our self-concept by imagining how others see and judge us. It's like other people are a mirror. This teenager's teachers and classmates keep calling her artistic and praising her drawings. She takes in that reflected view and starts to see herself as artistic. A common trap is mixing this up with George Herbert Mead's role-taking stages, since both ideas come from symbolic interactionism, the study of how people build meaning through everyday interaction.

questions.q: A 5-year-old plays 'doctor,' acting out how a doctor speaks to a patient, but cannot yet coordinate several roles at once the way players on a team must. Which stage in Mead's theory is this?
o: Preparatory stage
The preparatory stage is copying without understanding roles, which comes earlier.
Play stage
Correct: in the play stage, children take on one specific role at a time.
Game stage
The game stage requires tracking many roles at once.
Formal operational stage
This is a Piaget stage, not part of Mead's theory.
questions.x: George Herbert Mead described three stages of learning social roles. In the play stage, children take on the role of one specific person at a time, often a significant other (an important person in their life) or a familiar figure like a doctor. Playing doctor, acting out how a doctor talks, fits that. She can't yet keep track of many roles at once, which is what the game stage requires. The trap is picking game stage just because she's 'playing.'

questions.q: After failing an exam, a student concludes, 'The test was unfair and the professor dislikes me.' A student who thinks this way across many situations most likely has:
o: an internal locus of control
An internal locus credits your own effort and ability.
an external locus of control
Correct: blaming luck, others or circumstances is an external locus of control.
high self-efficacy
High self-efficacy means believing you can affect outcomes yourself.
a self-discrepancy between actual and ideal self
Nothing in the story compares the actual and ideal selves.
questions.x: Locus of control is where a person believes the causes of their outcomes lie. With an internal locus, you see your own effort and ability as the cause. With an external locus, you see luck, other people or circumstances as the cause. This student blames an unfair test and a professor who dislikes them, both outside forces, and does this across many situations. That steady pattern is an external locus of control. Blaming others isn't a sign of high self-esteem or confidence.

questions.q: Two students interpret the same handshake differently: one as respect, the other as a challenge. Which theory best emphasizes this variability?
o: Structural functionalism
Functionalism is macro-level and looks at how structures keep society stable.
Symbolic interactionism
Correct: meaning comes from how people interpret symbols, so one handshake can mean different things.
Conflict theory
Conflict theory is macro-level and focuses on power and inequality.
Demographic transition theory
This theory describes shifts in birth and death rates, not interaction.
questions.x: Symbolic interactionism is a small-scale (micro) theory about how people create meaning through symbols like words, gestures and objects. It says meaning isn't built into a symbol. People interpret and negotiate it as they interact. That's why the same handshake can read as respect to one student and as a challenge to another. Functionalism and conflict theory look at society as a whole, so they don't zoom in on how two people read a single gesture.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects social constructionism?
o: Social categories reflect fixed biological facts that societies merely discover.
This is biological determinism, which treats categories as fixed natural facts.
Categories such as 'adolescence' gain meaning through shared social agreement and vary across societies.
Correct: categories like adolescence get meaning from shared agreement and vary by society.
Social order depends mainly on each person's calculation of personal benefit.
This is rational choice theory: order comes from personal benefit calculations.
Social change occurs only through class struggle over resources.
This is a strict conflict-theory view, and 'only' is a warning sign.
questions.x: Social constructionism says categories like adolescence get their meaning because people agree on it together. Since people make those meanings, they differ across societies and change over time. Some cultures barely have an 'adolescence' stage at all. Constructed doesn't mean fake, though: these categories still shape laws, schools and lives in real ways. The other choices describe biological determinism (fixed facts), rational choice (personal benefit) and a strict conflict view (only class struggle).

questions.q: A group deliberately rejects mainstream values and organizes a lifestyle opposed to them. This group is a:
o: Subculture
A subculture differs from the mainstream but isn't defined by opposing it.
Reference group
A reference group is a standard you compare yourself to, not a group rejecting values.
Primary group
A primary group is defined by close, lasting ties, not opposition.
Counterculture
Correct: a counterculture actively opposes mainstream norms and values.
questions.x: This is a counterculture: a group that deliberately rejects mainstream values and builds a way of life against them. The key word is opposition. A subculture is the tempting wrong answer, because it's also a group that's different from the mainstream. But a subculture just has its own tastes or practices while living alongside the main culture, like a skateboarding or gaming community. It isn't trying to overturn mainstream values.

questions.q: Ritzer's concept of McDonaldization emphasizes which feature of modern society?
o: Spontaneity and emotional expression
Spontaneity is the opposite of the standardization McDonaldization describes.
Resistance to technological change
The concept relies on technology for control rather than resisting it.
Decline of formal organizations
Rationalization grows formal organizations rather than shrinking them.
Efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control
Correct: Ritzer's four features are efficiency, predictability, calculability and control.
questions.x: George Ritzer's McDonaldization takes Max Weber's idea of rationalization, which means replacing tradition with rules, efficiency and calculation, and says it's spreading through all of modern society. He named four features: efficiency (the fastest way to get things done), predictability (the same result everywhere), calculability (counting quantity over judging quality) and control (rules and technology directing people). It's named after a fast-food chain, but it describes schools, hospitals and workplaces too.

questions.q: In a low-mortality country, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 is described as:
o: Zero population growth immediately
Growth doesn't stop right away; a young age structure keeps it going for decades.
Replacement-level fertility
Correct: about 2.1 replaces two parents, plus a little for children who die young.
Demographic dividend
The demographic dividend is an economic boost from a large working-age group, not a fertility level.
Natural decrease
Natural decrease means deaths outnumber births, which a TFR of 2.1 wouldn't cause.
questions.x: A total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman has in her lifetime. A TFR of about 2.1 is called replacement-level fertility, because it lets each generation just replace itself. Two children replace the two parents, and the extra 0.1 covers children who die before having kids of their own. Two traps here. Replacement isn't exactly 2.0. And reaching 2.1 doesn't stop growth right away, because a young population keeps growing for decades (population momentum).
